story.hook: The Movers Locked My Furniture in Their Truck
story.script: When I moved across town, I chose a company that advertised a fixed price with no surprise fees. The estimator visited my apartment, photographed every room, counted the boxes, measured the staircase, and wrote down that the new building had an elevator. His quote included the truck, three movers, protective blankets, travel time, and four hours of labor. I signed it and paid the deposit. On moving day, the crew arrived forty minutes late but worked quickly. They wrapped the sofa, carried everything downstairs, and loaded the last box with thirty minutes left in the quoted window. At the new building, the driver parked beside the loading entrance and handed me a tablet. The total on the screen was nine hundred dollars more than the signed quote. He said there were extra charges for stairs, heavy furniture, blankets, fuel, and using the elevator. I pointed out that every one of those details was written on the estimator's form. The driver shrugged and said the office created the invoice, not him. Then he told me the truck would stay locked until I paid the full amount. My bed, work computer, clothes, and medication were all inside. I called the office. A manager said the signed quote only covered transportation and that the smaller print allowed operational fees. I asked her to email me the exact page she meant. She sent a different contract with my name typed at the top, but it did not have my signature. The date on it was also that morning, weeks after I had signed the real agreement. I told her I would pay the original balance immediately, but not charges added through a document I had never seen. She said the truck would leave for their storage yard in fifteen minutes. Fortunately, my new building's loading area had cameras and a security desk. I asked the guard to record the truck number and the conversation. Then I called the city's consumer protection office, whose number was printed on the moving permit displayed inside the truck windshield. The person who answered asked whether the mover was licensed and whether I had a written estimate. I read him the permit number and emailed both documents while we spoke. He noticed something I had missed. For local residential moves, that license required the company to give written notice before adding storage or holding a shipment over a price dispute. Their replacement contract did not count because it had been created after pickup and was unsigned. He asked me to put the call on speaker. The driver listened while the officer explained that taking the truck to storage without the required notice could trigger an immediate complaint against the company's license. The driver called his manager. A few minutes later, the manager called me back with a completely different tone. She said the invoice system had applied the wrong rate and sent a corrected bill matching the original quote. I paid it while everyone watched. The truck doors opened, and the crew unloaded every item without another argument. Before they left, the driver quietly showed me the tablet. The disputed charges had not disappeared; someone at the office had manually marked each one waived. I saved a screenshot. The next week, consumer protection contacted me for the emails, the fake contract, the camera timestamp, and that screenshot. Two other customers had reported the same tactic. The company eventually refunded my deposit as part of a settlement and had to change its written pricing process. They locked my furniture in a truck to force nine hundred extra dollars out of me. Instead, the permit in their own windshield unlocked the truck and their other complaints.
